feed.title: Neurotidy guides
feed.subtitle: Neurotidy makes free printable ADHD task cards, a free ADHD cleaning checklist and weekly cleaning planner, three free browser tools (a room reset timer, a chore breakdown and a task card maker), and plain-language guides for cleaning your home with ADHD, written under the pen name Mara Ellery at neurotidy.co.

entry.title: ADHD cups everywhere? Why it happens and the once-a-day fix
entry.summary: Cups left in every room are ADHD out of sight, out of mind, not laziness. Why the cup drops out of your head, and the once-a-day sweep that ends it.

entry.title: ADHD clothes chair pile: why it happens and how to clear it
entry.summary: The clothes chair holds what is too clean to wash and too worn to put away. With ADHD that pile has no home. Give it one, then clear five at a time.

entry.title: ADHD floordrobe: why clothes live on the floor, and the fix
entry.summary: A floordrobe is clothes living on the floor instead of in drawers. With ADHD, out of sight feels gone. How visible storage gets the floor clear again.

entry.title: Cleaning paralysis and ADHD: why you freeze and how to start
entry.summary: Cleaning paralysis is wanting to clean but not being able to start. With ADHD it is a task initiation problem, not laziness. Here is the tiny first step.

entry.title: Best time to do chores on ADHD meds: find your easy window
entry.summary: If you take ADHD medication, there is often a stretch of the day when starting chores feels easier. How to spot it and fit a five-minute reset inside.

entry.title: ADHD bathroom cleaning: a 5-minute reset that gets done
entry.summary: An ADHD bathroom cleaning routine that gets done: five minutes in a fixed order, right after your shower. Counter, sink, mirror, toilet, floor, out.

entry.title: Low-energy ADHD cleaning list: 6 tasks for bad brain days
entry.summary: What to clean with ADHD when you have no energy: six tiny tasks, no decisions, under ten minutes. Rinse a mug, tie the trash, clear the path to bed. Done.

entry.title: Why dishes pile up with ADHD (and what helps)
entry.summary: ADHD dishes pile up in the sink because every dish is four decisions stacked behind it, not laziness. Here's why it happens and what actually helps.

entry.title: Doom piling and ADHD: what a doom pile is, how to clear it
entry.summary: Doom piling means moving things into a pile instead of deciding where they go. A doom pile is the ADHD decision backlog it builds. Here is how to clear one.

entry.title: ADHD laundry: why the clean pile never gets folded
entry.summary: ADHD laundry folding is the hard part, not the washing. Here's why the clean basket sits for a week, and five ways to actually get clothes put away.

entry.title: The 5-minute ADHD evening cleaning reset (closing-shift method)
entry.summary: A 5-minute ADHD cleaning reset is a closing shift for your home: timer, surfaces, sink, tomorrow's setup. Here's why it works and the checklist.

entry.title: ADHD time blindness: why cleaning feels like forever
entry.summary: You avoid the kitchen because it feels like an hour. ADHD time blindness makes cleaning feel huge, but time it once and it's six minutes, not willpower.

entry.title: The ADHD cleaning checklist that actually works (room by room)
entry.summary: An ADHD cleaning checklist works when every line is one physical action, takes under five minutes, and is written down. Room by room version inside.

entry.title: ADHD body doubling: why you can clean when someone's just there
entry.summary: Body doubling means doing a task while someone else is simply present, and for ADHD brains that presence makes starting to clean dramatically easier.

entry.title: Doom pile vs hoarding: the difference, and the numbers behind it
entry.summary: A doom pile is deferred decisions. Hoarding disorder is different: one clinic study found about 20% of ADHD adults had real symptoms, versus 2% of others.

entry.title: Why is my room always messy? The ADHD answer nobody gave you
entry.summary: Why is my room always messy? Usually not laziness. ADHD traits rebuild the mess, so the fix is designing the room for your brain, not cleaning harder.

entry.title: An ADHD cleaning schedule that actually sticks
entry.summary: An ADHD cleaning schedule that actually sticks is short, anchored to habits you already have, and has a bad-day line. How to build one you keep running.

entry.title: ADHD object permanence: why out of sight is out of mind
entry.summary: ADHD object permanence and cleaning: why out of sight is out of mind, what research actually calls it (working memory), and the visible-storage fix.

entry.title: The bare-minimum ADHD cleaning day (for when it's all too much)
entry.summary: A bare minimum ADHD cleaning routine for when everything is too much: three anchor moments, ten minutes total, no deep clean. Enough to hold the line.

entry.title: How to declutter a doom pile step by step (ADHD method)
entry.summary: How to declutter a doom pile step by step with ADHD: one pile, a 10-minute timer, four boxes, no decisions. The sort that finally makes the pile shrink.

entry.title: What is the 1-3-5 rule for ADHD, and does it work for cleaning?
entry.summary: The 1-3-5 rule for ADHD: one big task, three medium, five small per day. Where it comes from, why a capped list suits ADHD, and how to run it on a messy house.
